newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican rebels claim army understated casualties.
newsitem.headline: Mexican rebels claim army understated casualties.

text.p: Mexico's Marxist guerrillas accused the army of covering up scores of casualties in a recent clash between rebels and army troops in the impoverished western state of Guerrero.
The left-wing Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) said in a statement late on Monday that at least 30 army troops were either injured or killed in Saturday's battle.
The military had said earlier that two of its soldiers were killed and three army medics wounded in the fight. It also said two rebels were killed, which the EPR acknowledged in its statement.
No one at the Defence Ministry was immediately available for comment on the statement.

"On May 24 ... a battle broke out between one of our units and several army units, resulting in at least 30 casualties for the federal army, the majority of which were fatalities," the EPR's military command in Guerrero said in the statement.

"The army's casualties were much higher than was officially reported -- a move to prevent morale from falling, but one which shows a total lack of respect for its soldiers' lives," said the statement, signed by Commander Hermenegildo.

Although the army said it had been ambushed by guerrillas, the EPR statement backed up reports by witnesses that the battle erupted when a convoy of army troops happened upon rebels distributing leaflets to motorists on a remote highway.

The clash was the first reported this year between the military and the EPR, which sprang up in late June 1996 calling for a Marxist popular uprising to overthrow the federal government of President Ernesto Zedillo.
After a series of attacks last summer that killed about 30 people, the group called a series of ceasefires late last year to carry out what it termed "armed propaganda" to drum up popular support.

But it warned recently that the army's stepped-up hunt for the rebels had led to sporadic clashes, which it said the government had covered up in a bid to convince Mexicans it had the guerrillas under control.
Saturday's clash became public when a taxi driver picked up a police radio transmission reporting the attack and confirming that the guerrillas had been distributing propaganda along the road.

"This time there were testimonies of the event that made it impossible to hide, as your forces have done on other occasions," the rebels said in a separate letter to Mexican Defence Minister Enrique Cervantes, also released on Monday.
